title: What tests are for
summary: Why teams pay for tests, the test pyramid and the testing trophy, what deserves a test, and your first xUnit tests graded against planted bugs.

steps.title: What a test suite buys you
body: A test is code that runs your code and fails loudly when the behaviour is wrong. A team pays for tests because they buy four things:

- **Safe change.** You refactor, upgrade a package or fix a bug, and 2,000 tests tell you in a minute that nothing else broke. Without them, every change is a gamble that someone pays for in production.
- **Fast feedback.** A unit test fails in milliseconds on your laptop. The same bug found by a customer costs a support ticket, an incident and a hotfix.
- **Design pressure.** Code that is hard to test is usually hard to use: too many dependencies, hidden inputs like the clock. Tests make that pain visible early.
- **Living documentation.** `Cost_is_free_from_50_euros` says what the code promises, and it can never go out of date, because it runs.

Tests are not free: they are code you read, run and maintain. A test that breaks on every refactor while catching nothing is a cost, not an asset. This topic is about writing the tests that pay for themselves.

Different kinds of test trade speed for realism. The classic **test pyramid** (many unit tests, fewer integration tests, a few end-to-end) and the newer **testing trophy** (static analysis at the base, integration tests as the widest part) are two ways to balance that. Pick a layer to compare them.

steps.prompt: A pull request registers a new service in `Program.cs` with the wrong lifetime, and the app throws at startup. All 900 unit tests pass. Which kind of test would have caught it?
options: An integration test that starts the app's real HTTP pipeline (TestServer) and calls one endpoint
Another unit test of the service class, with its dependencies mocked
A higher line-coverage target for the unit tests
A manual check by the reviewer
steps.explain: Unit tests build objects by hand, so they never run the app's dependency-injection setup. Only a test that boots the real pipeline sees wiring mistakes. That is the trophy's argument for many integration tests.

steps.prompt: Which layer is the right home for each test?
items: A discount of 10% rounds to the cent
`POST /orders` returns 400 when the body has no lines
A customer can sign up, pay and see the receipt in the browser
The EF Core query for overdue invoices returns the right rows
The checkout page works after a deploy to staging
steps.explain: Pure rules live in unit tests. Anything that crosses your process boundary (HTTP pipeline, SQL, JSON) belongs to integration tests. Whole user journeys through a deployed system are end-to-end, and you keep only a few because they are slow and flaky.

steps.title: What deserves a test
body: Test **behaviour through the public surface**, not lines of code. Good candidates, in order of value:
1. **Business rules and their boundaries**: free shipping from 50, a discount that caps at 30%, a late fee after 14 days. Bugs live on the boundary (`>` written where `>=` was meant).
2. **Error paths**: invalid input, a missing record, a dependency that times out. They are rarely clicked by hand, so they rot quietly.
3. **Anything that broke before**: a bug fix comes with the test that would have caught it (a *regression test*).
4. **Code that is changing**: a refactor is only safe with tests around the behaviour first.
Usually **not** worth a test: private methods on their own (test them through the public method that uses them), auto-properties, the framework itself (`List<T>.Add` works), and generated code.
```csharp fragment
public static class Shipping
// The rule: orders of 50 or more ship free, smaller ones pay 4.99.
public static decimal Cost(decimal total) => total >= 50m ? 0m : 4.99m;
One test at 20 and one at 80 both pass with `>=` *and* with `>`. Only a test at exactly **50** tells them apart.

steps.prompt: Which of these deserve their own tests? Select all that apply.
options: The rule that a coupon cannot bring a total below zero
What happens when the payment provider times out
A bug from last sprint where Feb 29 broke the renewal date
That `public string Name { get; set; }` stores the name
A private helper `FormatCents`, called directly through reflection
steps.explain: Rules, error paths and past bugs carry risk. An auto-property has none. A private helper is tested through the public method that uses it: reaching in with reflection ties the test to the implementation, so it breaks on every refactor.

steps.title: Your first xUnit tests
body: **xUnit.net v3** is the most used test framework for new .NET projects. A test is a public method marked `[Fact]` in a public class, and `Assert` fails it with a clear message:
```csharp
public class ShippingTests
[Fact]
public void Small_orders_pay_for_shipping()
decimal cost = Shipping.Cost(20m);
Assert.Equal(4.99m, cost);      // expected first, then actual
public static class Shipping
public static decimal Cost(decimal total) => total >= 50m ? 0m : 4.99m;
Press **Try it** under the sample: it runs the real xUnit runner. Change `4.99m` to `5m` and run it again to see a failure message.
`Assert.Equal(expected, actual)` prints both values when it fails (`Expected: 4.99, Actual: 0`), which is why the order matters.

**How these exercises are graded.** You write the tests. The dojo runs them with the real xUnit runner against the correct code (they must all pass), then against copies of the code with one bug planted in each, called **mutants**. A good suite fails on every mutant. That is *mutation testing*, the most honest measure of a test suite there is, and you will meet its real tool, Stryker.NET, later in this topic.

steps.prompt: Complete the test so xUnit finds it and it checks that an order of exactly 50 ships free.
steps.explain: `[Fact]` marks a test with no parameters. `Assert.Equal` compares expected with actual. 50 is the boundary itself, the one value that catches `>` written for `>=`.

steps.title: Tests that catch the bugs
prompt: Write the tests for this code, which the dojo compiles beside yours:
public static decimal Cost(decimal total) => total >= 50m ? 0m : 4.99m;
Write a public class `ShippingTests` with at least **three** `[Fact]` tests.
**Run checks** runs them on this code (they must pass), then on three copies with a bug planted in each. Each bug must make at least one of your tests fail. Think about the boundary.

target: public static decimal Cost(decimal total) => total >= 50m ? 0m : 4.99m;

mutants.name: the free-shipping boundary moved to above 50
big orders pay too
mutants.hint: Test an order that should ship free.

hints: The starter catches one bug already. Which planted bug would still pass it?
One test must sit exactly on the boundary: `Shipping.Cost(50m)` must be `0m`.
Add `Assert.Equal(0m, Shipping.Cost(50m));` in its own `[Fact]`, and one just below (49.99) that still pays.
steps.explain: Three tests, three different reasons to fail. The boundary test is the one people forget, and the one that catches the most common bug in business code.
